Voglio che vi sposiate a Sorrento
You use the present subjunctive after verbs of wanting, opinion, hope and necessity (voglio che tu venga, penso che sia vero, bisogna che partiamo).
I want you to get married in Sorrento.
I think Giulia is too thin.
I hope it'll be less cold tomorrow.
It's important for the families to get to know each other.
To form the regular present subjunctive: parli, prenda, parta, finisca.
To use the irregular forms: sia, abbia, vada, faccia, venga, possa, voglia, debba, stia, dia, sappia.
To use the subjunctive after wanting: voglio che, preferisco che, desidero che.
To use the subjunctive after opinion and hope: penso che, credo che, spero che, mi sembra che.
To use the subjunctive after impersonal expressions: bisogna che, è importante che, è meglio che.
To know when NOT to use the subjunctive: same subject → infinitive (voglio partire).
January in Sibiu. It's minus twelve. Giulia and Matei are in Doina's kitchen when the phone rings: it's Grandma Assunta, from Naples.
Giulia, my girl! How are you? Is it cold up there?
Grandma, it's minus twelve! But Matei's mother makes us eat loads.
Good. Listen, I've spoken to the priest. I want you to get married in Sorrento, in the church where I got married.
In Sorrento? Grandma, we haven't decided anything yet…
Exactly. Somebody has to decide! And I think September is the best month: it's not too hot.
(quietly) But my parents would like a party in Sibiu too…
I heard that, Matei! All right: first Sorrento, then Sibiu. But it's important for the two families to meet first. I want your mother to come to Naples for Easter.
I think that's an excellent idea, signora.
And one more thing. I hope you'll learn a bit of Neapolitan before the wedding. I don't want my cousins making fun of you.
I'll do my best, Signora Assunta.
Call me Grandma. You're family now. And Giulia, eat! I think you're too thin.
(laughs) Grandma, you say exactly the same things as Matei's mother!
(that) they get to know each other
"ti prendano in giro" = make fun of you
"farò del mio meglio" = I'll do my best
SI-a = two syllables, stress on I: "see-a". SEE-a-no.
Double consonants: AB-bya, FAT-cha; VA-da (single). Stress on the first syllable.
Hard G before A: VEN-ga, TEN-ga. Not "ven-ja"!
Stress on "YA": spo-ZYA-te. Likewise: par-LYA-te, an-DYA-te.

The subjunctive is the mood of subjectivity: you use it when talking about what you want, think, hope or need — not about certain facts. It partly corresponds to the Romanian conjunctive ("vreau SĂ VII").
Voglio che Matei venga a cena.
As in Romanian: "vreau ca tu să vii" = "voglio che tu venga". The difference: Italian also uses the subjunctive after "I think that" (penso che sia), where Romanian uses the indicative ("cred că e").
The persons io, tu, lui have the same form — that's why the pronoun is often added: che io parli, che tu parli.
Watch the swap: -ARE takes I (parli), while -ERE / -IRE take A (prenda, parta). It's the opposite of the present!
Tip: many are formed from the "io" form of the present: vengo → venga, faccio → faccia, dico → dica, vado → vada.

penso che, credo che, mi sembra che, ritengo che
After "so che", "sono sicuro che", "è vero che" (certainty) you use the INDICATIVE: "So che è vero."
If the two verbs have the SAME subject, use the infinitive (with "di" after verbs of opinion):
Not "Voglio che io parta"! When I want and I leave: "Voglio partire."

On their first day at the Brukenthal Museum, Matei and Giulia walked into a workshop full of light on the third floor of the palace, with windows looking out over the snow-covered Great Square. Twelve Italian paintings were waiting for them on the easels: saints, landscapes, a portrait of a woman with a blue veil.
The head of the workshop, Mrs Popescu, spoke perfect Italian. "I hope you'll feel at home here," she said. "And I hope the cold won't make you run away. The heating works… when it feels like it."

The portrait of the woman with the blue veil was the most damaged painting: someone had badly repainted it in the nineteenth century. "I want the two of you to restore it together," said Mrs Popescu. "I think it's the hardest, but also the most beautiful." Giulia looked at it for a long time. "She has your mother's eyes," she said quietly to Matei.

The work was wonderful, but the real show was at home. Every evening at dinner Doina and Giulia had a strange conversation: Doina spoke Romanian, Giulia answered in Italian, Matei translated, and Ion ate in silence, smiling.

"Tell her I want her to eat more," Doina would say. "My mother wants you to eat more," Matei translated. "Tell her I think she cooks too much," Giulia replied. Matei translated diplomatically: "Giulia says the food is delicious."

Then the wedding question began. On the phone every Sunday Grandma Assunta had a new idea: "I want at least two hundred guests." "The lunch must last six hours." "It's important that the dress is my mother's."

Doina, at dinner, had her own ideas: "I want sarmale at the wedding." "The cousins from Cluj must come too." "It's important that we dance the hora." Matei translated everything, in both directions, and by evening he had a headache.
Ion, on the other hand, had just one request, which he made one evening in Italian, with his terrible accent: "I want there to be pălincă." Everyone laughed, but nobody said no.

One night Giulia couldn't sleep. "Matei, I'm afraid our mothers will argue. I think they want two different weddings." Matei thought about it. "What if we had just one wedding, but with both things? Sarmale and pastiera. Hora and tarantella."
Giulia looked at him in the dark. "Do you think it's possible?" "I think it's the only solution. We just need the two grandmothers to meet. If they like each other, the rest will follow."

The next day they made a three-way video call: Sibiu, Naples and Florence, where Graziella had offered to be the "neutral referee". On the screen, the eighty-six-year-old Romanian grandmother and the ninety-one-year-old Neapolitan grandmother looked at each other for the first time, in silence.

Then Matei's grandmother picked up a plate of sarmale and showed it to the camera. Assunta picked up a plate of pastiera and did the same. They didn't need translators. They both laughed at the same moment, with the same grandmotherly laugh.
"I think they've understood each other," said Graziella from Florence. "Now you just need to decide on the date. And I hope you'll invite me, because I dance the tarantella better than both of them."
